_comment: Landing FAQ. One source for the React accordion, the no-JS HTML, the FAQPage JSON-LD (src/landing/staticHtml.ts) and llms.txt (scripts/gen_agent_index.py). Answers: 1-3 sentences, only what Cortex does today.

items.a: Cortex is an open-source (MIT) MCP server that lets any AI agent train a robot. The agent describes its arm and a custom environment or layout; Cortex builds it in MuJoCo, collects demonstrations, trains an imitation-learning policy (ACT) and evaluates it, then carries the policy to the physical arm to train further and deploy. It is built on LeRobot, MuJoCo, ACT and the SO-101 (SO-ARM101) arm.

items.q: How do I train a robot policy with an AI agent?
items.a: Connect your agent to the Cortex MCP server, then ask for the task in plain words. The agent calls cortex.start_intake and cortex.update_intake to describe the arm, objects and goal, cortex.build_simulation for the MuJoCo scene, cortex.start_agent_collection for demonstrations, cortex.create_dataset_version and cortex.propose_training_job; training (behaviour cloning with ACT or SmolVLA) starts after a person approves the GPU job in the studio.

items.q: Can Claude Code train a robot?
items.a: Yes, in simulation. Run claude mcp add --transport http cortex http://localhost:3000/mcp and ask Claude Code to teach the arm a task; it calls cortex.* tools and reads the results. It never sends motor commands: Cortex validates every target and executes it with inverse kinematics, and the simulator decides whether an attempt succeeded.

items.q: How do I collect demonstrations for an SO-101 with LeRobot in MuJoCo?
items.a: cortex.start_agent_collection runs autonomous attempts in fresh simulator seeds, planned by a vision-language model or by the scripted IK oracle (labelled as such); only simulator-verified successes are saved, as LeRobotDataset v3 episodes. Your agent can also drive the arm itself with cortex.robot_start_episode and the cortex.robot_* tools, or import existing recordings from the Hugging Face Hub with cortex.import_demonstrations.

items.q: How do I evaluate a robot policy in simulation?
items.a: cortex.evaluate_learned_policy runs a trained checkpoint in three seeded MuJoCo branches (baseline, shifted object, dim lighting) on held-out seeds. Success rates are reported with 95% Wilson confidence intervals, and cortex.compare_experiments gives branch-by-branch deltas and p-values between runs.

items.q: How do I improve an ACT policy with targeted demonstrations or RL?
items.a: cortex.improve_policy finds the weakest measured condition of the latest evaluation, collects new demonstrations there in fresh seeds, builds a new dataset version and proposes retraining. Reinforcement learning is not an agent tool yet: the planned RL sandbox tunes the pick-and-place skill under domain randomization, its successful rollouts become demonstrations that retrain ACT, and any uplift is shown as a labelled estimate.

items.q: Is there an MCP server for robotics?
items.a: Cortex is one: a Model Context Protocol server over streamable HTTP at http://localhost:3000/mcp, exposing intake, simulation, data collection, dataset, training, evaluation and improvement tools as cortex.*. The same tools answer on REST at http://localhost:8000/api/tools, and calls are attributed to the agent in the audit log.

items.q: Can the agent train and deploy on the physical robot arm?
items.a: That is where the loop leads: after simulation, the policy moves to the physical SO-101 to keep training on real demonstrations and then perform the task. Today the whole loop runs in MuJoCo, and a real arm runs a policy only through a local bridge with an operator present, joint, velocity and workspace limits, a watchdog and an e-stop; the API and MCP cannot drive the hardware directly.
